doc.title: Wayne Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

chapter: Opening and the music business today
title: Being a trombonist in New York in 2002
summary: Andre says the business is worse than ever, blaming synthesizers and a shortage of work for older players, though he writes more now.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well it’s a pleasure to meet you. And I’m wondering what it’s like in 2002 to be a full time trombonist in New York City.
For me not too bad because I have a good pension. But for younger players it’s a scuffle. Are you talking about the music business in general or are you talking about the jazz music business?
You know I’m talking about in general right now.

In general. I think I’ve never seen it worse. We’ve been killed for many years by synthetic music and California, which does the majority of the movies — they don’t do all of them but they do probably 95% of the movies — the movies have kind of gotten away from synthetic music. You know what I mean by synthetic music, don’t you?
Music made by synthesizers. Music that doesn’t breathe. I hate it.

I mean it has its place in a certain place, but it’s like when I do a jazz gig or whatever with electric piano, the thing I don’t like about it is the instrument never seems to breathe. I like to hear space in music.
Right. There’s no silence at all.

Yeah. And there’s no nuance either, particularly with volume. You don’t hear pianissimo, you don’t hear forte, you just hear this one blaring sound all the time. But this is my observation on hearing it. But to get back to the business, I think I’m playing as well today as I’ve ever played in my life but I must be honest, the recording business in New York City, and the theater business — I wouldn’t want to do a Broadway show anyway © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

— but the thing is most of it is geared toward younger musicians. As well it should be. I had my time. And I think I’m capable and qualified to do a lot more but I’m saying a lot of younger leaders come in and they’ve got their guys so to speak and with the older leaders that I work for kind of drift off and I might be still playing but they’re not still writing so I sit home and I’m not working that much, quite frankly, at all. But I’m doing a lot of writing. I have my own band and I’m enjoying life. I’m in a nice place.
